title: CNN, Axios and others join Google's AI news licensing program
subtitle: Google's News AI pilot — once a 20-publisher commercial test — now covers more than 400 outlets globally, with new entrants getting a Search Console earnings widget tied to Gemini and AI Overviews contributions.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google said on October 15 that CNN, Axios, and additional publishers have joined its News AI commercial pilot, bringing the program's total to more than 400 publications globally. Google launched the pilot in late 2025 with a small set of partners, among them The Washington Post, The Guardian, Der Spiegel, and El País, to test embedding AI-generated article overviews and audio briefings in Google News, with attribution and links back to the originals. New entrants receive a dedicated earnings widget in Search Console that pays when their content contributes to Gemini responses, AI Overviews, and AI Mode results.

The program's financial design is deliberately different from the lump-sum licensing deals OpenAI has signed with News Corp, Axel Springer, the Financial Times, and the Associated Press. Google pays per contribution, and critics quoted in Digiday have called the terms a 'black box' with early payments 'peanuts' next to ad revenue. There is also a quid-pro-quo element — The Information previously reported that Google is asking participants to grant broader usage rights, including the right to use content for AI training, and that publishers who refuse may eventually lose the annual fee from Google News Showcase, which Google plans to end.

For CNN and Axios, this is a bet in both directions. CNN sits inside the Google-owned traffic funnel that is being hollowed out by AI Overviews, so some share of that re-flow is better than none; Axios, which has its own OpenAI deal to fund new local newsrooms in Pittsburgh, Kansas City, Boulder and Huntsville, can run both licensing streams in parallel. The 400-publication milestone also puts Google's AI news footprint between News Showcase (2,800+ titles) and the handful of large lump-sum licensing deals its rivals have struck — mid-sized by publisher count, but with a payment model that scales with AI query volume rather than contract value.

For learners: 'licensing' in AI content deals is now at least three different things. Lump-sum training-data deals pay once, up front, and often include ongoing API access to the publisher's archive. Per-use payouts (Google's model here) pay only when the content shows up in a specific AI product's answers, and the publisher has to trust the vendor's metering. And the Showcase-style arrangement pays for curation and surface placement, not AI use at all. When you read 'Publisher X signs AI deal,' the useful next question is which of the three it is — the headline rarely says.
